title: Should you bid what it is worth?
hook: You pay your own bid, so bidding full value earns nothing. How far below should you go?

knows: in a second-price auction you bid your value
expected value: a payoff times its chance
doesNotKnow: that when you pay your own bid, the best bid is well below your value

misconception: In a first-price sealed auction you should bid what the item is worth to you.
objective: The learner can explain that in a first-price auction a lower bid keeps more per win but wins less often, and find that with value $80 against a rival bidding half of an evenly spread $0-100 value the best bid is $40 (expected $32).

claims.text: Against a rival who bids half of a value spread evenly on $0 to $100, a bid of b wins with chance b/50 up to $50, and every time above $50.
claims.source: Lesson rule: rival value uniform on [0,100], rival bid = value/2, so rival bid uniform on [0,50]; P(rival bid < b) = min(b,50)/50 (ties have probability 0). Builder's seeded Monte Carlo (mulberry32-style, 200,000 draws) gives 0.80 win chance at $40. Demo.tsx winChance. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own derivation: rival bid uniform on [0,50], P(win) = min(b,50)/50. Own LCG Monte Carlo (400,000 draws, scratchpad fc22/bid.mjs): 0.801 at $40, 1 at $50 and $60.

claims.text: With value $80, expected profit (80 minus bid, times the win chance) is $0 at a bid of $80, $30 at $50, $20 at $60 and $32 at $40, the highest of any bid.
claims.source: Builder's node grid over whole-dollar bids 0..100 (scratchpad ncm-e01-checks/check.mjs): (80-b)*min(b,50)/50; max 32 at b=40; 30 at 50, 20 at 60, 0 at 80. Calculus: for b<=50, d/db (80b - b^2)/50 = 0 at b=40. Demo.tsx expected and BEST. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own grid (0.01 steps, 0..100): (80-b)min(b,50)/50 maximal at b = 40.00 with $32; $30 at 50, $20 at 60, $0 at 80; $31.98 at 39 and 41.

claims.text: From $80 down to $50 the bid still wins every time; below $50 each dollar shaved costs 2 points of win chance.
claims.source: From c1: win chance is 1 for b >= 50, and b/50 below, which falls 0.02 per dollar. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): From c1: chance 1 for b >= 50; slope 1/50 = 2 points per dollar below 50.

claims.text: With two bidders whose values are spread evenly, bidding half your value is the equilibrium of the first-price auction.
claims.source: Standard result for two bidders with independent uniform private values: the symmetric equilibrium bid is v/2. W. Vickrey, Journal of Finance 16(1), 8-37 (1961); E&K ch. 9 (first-price auctions; section unconfirmed). Consistent with c2: the best reply to a rival bidding half is $40, half of $80. Citation from memory; fact-checker confirms. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Own derivation: against a rival bidding v/2 (v uniform 0..100), the best reply for every value v = 1..100 is v/2 (grid search, max deviation 0.000), so bidding half is a symmetric equilibrium (the standard symmetric one). Vickrey, J. Finance 16(1):8-37 (1961) confirmed as bibliographic data via search snippets; paper NOT opened. E&K ch. 9 (Auctions) placement agrees with my knowledge; section not checked.

claims.text: The stage is a model: one rival, values spread evenly, and the rival's bidding rule known.
claims.source: Modelling choice stated in the reveal. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-14 (pass 22): Convention, on stage: chip "Worth $80 to you · rival bids half of a $0-100 value"; reveal "A model: one rival, values spread evenly."

recall.question: In a sealed auction where the winner pays their own bid, what happens if you bid exactly what the item is worth to you?
options: You gain nothing even when you win
recall.why: Paying your full value leaves nothing over; a lower bid keeps something per win at the cost of winning less often, and the best bid balances the two.
